label: Summer camp

what_happens.title: What happens at camp
goals: Camp is a place for outdoor fun with a group
Day camp goes home, overnight camp sleeps in cabins
what_happens.parentSkill: Look at the camp schedule together and pick the activity your child is most curious about.

who_is_there.title: Who is at camp
goals: Counselors lead and look after the group
Nurses and directors help when needed
who_is_there.parentSkill: Tell your child the counselor is the first person to go to for anything, from a scraped knee to a sad feeling.

what_i_do.title: What I do at camp
goals: Drink water, wear sunscreen and stay with the group
what_i_do.parentSkill: Pack together and label everything, so your child knows what is in the bag.

if_scared.title: If I miss home
goals: Activities can feel hard at first
Calm tools: a letter from home, a busy activity, talking to a counselor
if_scared.parentSkill: Name homesickness before camp: 'You might miss home. That means you love home. It gets easier when you get busy.'

rehearsal.title: Let's get ready for camp
goals: Practise a name game and a camp song
rehearsal.parentSkill: Do a practice camp day in the garden or park: snack, game, water break and a song.

steps: Pack the camp bag with clothes, sunscreen and a water bottle
Arrive at camp and check in with a counselor
Meet the group and learn the names
Do activities like swimming, crafts, games and hikes
Rest, play and sing camp songs
Go home, or sleep in a cabin at an overnight camp
sensory: warm sun and the smell of sunscreen
a cabin bunk bed that creaks
honestyNotes: Homesickness is very common, especially at overnight camp; never promise the child will not miss home, and never promise a pick-up 'any time' unless the family means it. Activities can feel hard at first. Let the parent say if it is day camp or overnight camp.

fallbackAnswer: Lots of campers miss home, and that is normal.
Reading your note from home and getting busy can help.
Many campers are new, and friends at camp often happen fast.
You can start with the name game.
Counselors look after your group all day.
There is a camp nurse too.

questionButtons.text: Do I have to swim in the lake?
fallbackAnswer: Lifeguards watch the water, and kids swim where it is right for them.
You can say, I want to stay where I can stand.
Yes, camp is outside, so there are bugs.
Bug spray helps, and most bugs just buzz by.
At day camp you sleep at home.
At overnight camp, you sleep in a cabin with your group and a counselor.
[[GROWNUP]] and the camp will tell you the plan for calls or letters.
The counselor can always reach [[GROWNUP]] if needed.

questionButtons.text: What if an activity is too hard?
fallbackAnswer: You can watch first, or try a little bit.
Counselors help, and it is okay to say, not today.

questionButtons.text: What if I don't like the food?
fallbackAnswer: There are usually a few choices, and you can say no thank you.
Drinking water is important too.
Bumps and scrapes happen at camp. Tell your counselor straight away.
The camp nurse has bandages and helps.

techniques.label: A note from home
techniques.how: Hide a short note in the bag to read when missing home.

techniques.label: Practising the name game
techniques.how: Practise saying your name and one thing you like.

techniques.label: Watching first
techniques.how: Watch an activity first, then try a small part.

techniques.label: Water breaks
techniques.how: Drink water at every activity change.

techniques.label: Telling the counselor
techniques.how: Go to the counselor for any problem, big or small.

techniques.label: Getting busy
techniques.how: When homesick, join the next activity; busy helps feelings shrink.

techniques.label: A practice night away
techniques.how: Before overnight camp, try a night at a relative's house.

techniques.label: Bug spray and sunscreen
techniques.how: Put on bug spray and sunscreen together each morning.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Say my name in the name game

pain: If you get a scrape, tell your counselor. The nurse helps.
Bumps happen at camp, and they get better.
sensory: Bugs buzz, and most of them just fly by.
Camp songs are loud and silly.
strangers: Your counselor's job is to look after you.
You can tell a counselor anything.
separation: Missing home is normal. It means you love home.
Read your note when you miss me.
unknown: Check in, meet your group, then the first activity.
You can ask, what are we doing next?
love: I'm proud of you for trying camp.
I love you, and I will be here.

Camp is a place where kids play outside, try new things and make friends.
First [[CHILD]] checks in and meets a counselor.
Then the group learns each other's names with a fun game.
Before bed, here is a story about a young raccoon called Rory.
Rory was going to Camp Pinecone by the lake.
First Rory met the counselor, a tall deer called Juniper.
Then the group played a name game, clap, clap, Rory!
Next they made bead bracelets and splashed in the shallow lake.
After lunch, they rested in the shade.
Then they went on a short hike and found a feather.
In the evening, they sang a silly song about a moose.
Rory's tummy hurt from laughing.
Camp felt big and new, and also fun.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next there are activities, like crafts, swimming, sports and hikes.
After that comes lunch, a rest and more games.
There are camp songs and cheers.
Last, at day camp everyone goes home, and at overnight camp everyone sleeps in cabins.
[[CHILD]] can ask the counselor, what are we doing next?

They know the rules and keep everyone safe.

Juniper the deer was the group counselor.
If you need anything, come to me, said Juniper.
The camp nurse was a gentle tortoise with a bag of bandages.
Rory's group had a beaver, two rabbits and a quiet otter.
The otter looked nervous, just like Rory felt.
At crafts, Rory passed the otter some beads.
Thanks, said the otter, I am Ollie.
By lunch, Rory and Ollie were sitting together.
The group made up a team cheer.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
The other campers are kids of a similar age.
Many of them are new too, and some are nervous.
Friends at camp can happen fast, over a craft or a game.
A cabin or group becomes like a little team.

Try again, said Juniper, and the next one hit the edge of the target.

At camp, some kids feel homesick.
Homesick means missing home and family.
It often comes at quiet times, like rest or bedtime.
Homesickness is normal, and it usually gets smaller when the body is busy.
Some activities can feel scary or hard, like deep water or high ropes.
In the story, Rory the raccoon felt homesick at rest time.
Rory missed Mama and the cosy den.
Rory's eyes got wet.
Juniper the deer sat beside Rory.
Juniper did not say, you will not miss home.
Juniper said, lots of campers miss home, and it means you love your family.
Rory found the little note Mama had packed.
It said, I am proud of you, have fun.
Rory took a slow breath.
Then Ollie called, come on, we are making a dam.
Worried and brave can happen at the same time.
Saying, I want to watch first, is okay.
Bugs, heat and loud noises can feel like a lot sometimes.
Counselors know how to help.
[[CHILD]] can read the note from home and take slow breaths.
[[CHILD]] can tell a counselor, I miss home.

Camp is designed to stretch kids a little: new activities, new people and more independence.
Counselors are trained to keep groups safe, run activities and help with homesickness.
Overnight camp adds cabins, campfires and sometimes no phones, which feels strange at first and often becomes the best part.
Most kids say the first day is the hardest.
[[CHILD]] can choose one new activity to try that week.
Counselors are often older teens or young adults who went to camp themselves.
Camps have directors, nurses and lifeguards, and they all talk to each other.
Groups are usually by age, so campers have things in common.
Making friends at camp is easier because everyone starts at the same time.
[[CHILD]] can share one fun fact during the name game.
Staying with the group and following the buddy system is how camps keep track of everyone.
Hydration and sun protection matter more than kids think; headaches often mean thirst.
New activities can feel awkward the first time and fun by the third.
Being kind to a camper who is alone is how many camp friendships start.
[[CHILD]] can keep a camp journal with one highlight a day.
Almost every camper feels homesick at some point; counselors expect it and have tricks for it.
Homesickness usually peaks in the first day or two and at bedtime.
Keeping busy, writing a letter home and talking about it all help.
[[CHILD]] and [[GROWNUP]] can agree a plan before camp about calls or letters, so there are no surprises.
[[CHILD]] can count the activities left in the day instead of the days left at camp.
Packing your own bag, with a list, makes it easier to find things at camp.
For overnight camp, practising a night away at a relative's house first builds confidence.
Pre-addressed envelopes make writing home simple.
Talking to a kid who has been to that camp can answer the real questions.
[[CHILD]] can pick one goal for camp, like learning to paddle a canoe.
